Mass Media. Systems of communication and cultural distribution that reach millions of people simultaneously, including newspapers, radio, television, film, and digital platforms. Emerging from nineteenth-century printing technology and twentieth-century electrical innovations, mass media became the dominant means through which modern societies distribute information, entertainment, and ideology.

Modern mass media emerged from the combination of industrialization, printing press improvements, and electrical technologies such as radio, film, and television that could reach mass audiences simultaneously across vast distances. Mass media transformed public discourse. Newspapers became the primary source of political information. Radio and television brought real-time events into homes, creating shared national and international moments.

Mass media became intimately connected to advertising and consumer capitalism. Mass media provided audiences while advertising provided revenue, binding entertainment to commercial messaging and shaping consumer desires. It enabled standardization and homogenization of culture by distributing the same messages, entertainment, and values across diverse geographic and social groups, eroding local particularities.

Mass media created celebrity culture and star systems. Film and television made actors, musicians, and personalities into cultural icons with unprecedented influence over public taste, morality, and politics. Mass media became targets of political manipulation as governments and corporate interests used it to shape opinion, suppress dissent, and construct ideological narratives, particularly during wartime.

The centralized control of media by profit-driven corporations and governments transformed mass media into a powerful force shaping public opinion, consumer behavior, and cultural values—both democratizing information access and enabling unprecedented manipulation of collective consciousness. It connects to advertising the economic engine that funded mass media and shaped its content, to consumer culture the cultural system mass media both reflected and aggressively promoted, and to the broader transformation of modern societies through technology and communication.
